What is this?

International reserves are the dollars and other foreign assets held by the Central Bank. They work as a cushion: they let the country pay its foreign debts and calm the exchange rate in a crisis. That is why Brazil's public-sector net external debt is negative - the reserves are larger than what the state owes abroad.

The current account adds up trade in goods and services plus income sent abroad (profits, interest) and received. A negative number (deficit) means the country spent more abroad than it earned and needs to be financed with foreign money. A small deficit financed by long-term investment is normal for an emerging economy.

Foreign direct investment (IDP) is money that foreign companies bring to build or buy businesses in Brazil. It is the most stable way to finance a current-account deficit, unlike short-term financial flows that can leave quickly. Values are shown as 12-month totals to remove monthly noise.
